newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taipei cautions on plan for anti-Japanese action.
newsitem.headline: Taipei cautions on plan for anti-Japanese action.

text.p: Taiwan's foreign ministry appealed for calm on Saturday after a group of ex-convicts reaffirmed plans to destroy a Japanese-built lighthouse on a disputed East China Sea island.

"The government completely understands the patriotism of our people, but this kind of international dispute has to be handled with extreme calm," deputy Foreign Minister Cheng Chien-jen was quoted by the state-run Central News Agency as saying.

A group of paroled criminals, mostly former navy divers, said on Thursday they would embark on a mission to bomb the lighthouse built by Japanese rightists in July to symbolise Japanese control of one of the disputed Diaoyu Islands.
Tung Nie-tai, head of a private prisoners' rehabilitation centre to which group members belong, reaffirmed the plan on state television on Saturday.
"They will use either explosives or gas to bomb the lighthouse," he said.
Tung said the mission would take place between September 23 and 28. Up to 30 people had volunteered to join the bomb squad since it was formed on Thursday.
"We are launching the mission out of love for our country, so I hope the government does not interfere," Tung said.

A festering dispute over the Diaoyus, called the Senkakus in Japanese, erupted in July after the right-wing Japan Youth Federation erected a lighthouse there, angering rival claimants Taiwan and China.
The row intensified in recent days when Tokyo sent patrol ships to repel private Taiwan vessels that tried to approach the islands.
Foreign minister John Chang declined to comment on the planned bombing mission.
"I only found out about it through media reports. I can't comment because I don't know the real situation," he said.
"While our people should remain calm and rational, we also hope the Japan side would practise self-control," Chang added.
Taipei had said it would negotiate with Tokyo in order to solve the dispute, but no additional talks have been scheduled since a group of Japanese officials came to Taiwan in August.
Japan agreed during the August talks to halt plans to further assert Tokyo's claim to the islands.
